opus-5.5.text:
I think part of the reason is that "world model" has become a kind of umbrella term that different communities project their own goals onto. If you talk to someone from robotics or control, a world model is something quite concrete: given the current state and an action, can you predict the next state well enough to plan? If you talk to people in video generation, a world model often just means a model that can generate realistic, temporally consistent video, maybe with some interactivity. And if you talk to people coming from cognitive science, or someone like Yann, it means something deeper: an internal representation of how the world works that supports reasoning, planning, and common sense, and it doesn't necessarily need to produce pixels at all.

So the same phrase covers a predictive model, a generative model, a simulator, and a representation learning objective. These overlap, but they're not the same thing, and people talk past each other.

The second reason is that the "world" itself is hard to pin down. What level of abstraction are we modeling? Physics at the pixel level? Objects and their interactions? Other agents' intentions? Social dynamics? Humans have models at all of these levels simultaneously, and we switch between them effortlessly. When we say an AI system has a world model, we usually only mean one slice of that, but the word suggests the whole thing.

And third, I think we lack a good way to evaluate it. With language models you can at least run benchmarks and see whether the answers are right. With world models, a beautiful video doesn't tell you whether the model understands anything. It might be memorizing appearance statistics. The real test is whether it helps you act, plan, and generalize to situations you haven't seen, and that's much harder to measure. When you can't measure something cleanly, it's hard to define it cleanly too.

Personally, I lean toward thinking of a world model as something that's fundamentally about understanding and prediction in a useful representation space, in service of acting in the world, rather than just generation. Generation can be a useful training signal or a nice interface, but it's not the goal in itself. Still, I think it's healthy that the definition is contested right now. It means the field is still figuring out what the right problem actually is.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls “world model” an umbrella term that different communities project their goals onto, then distinguishes the varied models and objectives they use. This communicates that the term describes a goal rather than one specific technical approach or algorithm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the difficulty comes from the fact that "world model" is a term that sits at the intersection of several very different traditions, and each one brings its own baggage.

If you come from reinforcement learning, a world model is a very specific thing. It's a learned simulator. You have an agent, you have an environment, and the world model predicts the next state given the current state and an action, so you can plan or train inside the model instead of in the real world. That's a clean, almost engineering definition.

If you come from cognitive science or neuroscience, a world model is something much broader. It's the internal representation an animal or a person carries around that lets them anticipate what will happen, reason about causes, fill in what they can't see. That definition is about understanding, not about pixel prediction.

And then in the last couple of years, the generative AI community started using the phrase to describe video generation models. People watch a model generate a realistic clip of a ball rolling off a table and say, look, it has learned a world model. But the model was trained to produce plausible frames, not to be correct about physics or to be useful for an agent. So the word is being stretched to cover a very different capability.

So when someone asks "what is a world model," you're really getting at least three questions at once. Is it a simulator for planning? Is it an internal representation that supports understanding? Or is it a generative model of observations? These overlap, but they are not the same thing, and the evaluation criteria for each are different.

I'd add one more reason it's hard. Our own intuition about what counts as "understanding the world" is fuzzy. We know a model that generates a video with six fingers hasn't fully understood hands, but we have no agreed-upon test for when it has. So the definition keeps being driven by whatever the most impressive demo of the moment happens to be, instead of by a stable scientific criterion. Personally, I find it more productive to stop arguing about the label and ask concrete questions. Does the representation support prediction? Does it support counterfactuals? Does it transfer to tasks it wasn't trained on? Those are things you can actually measure.

r001.rationale: The response says “world model” spans several traditions and capabilities, but it does not explain that the term names a goal rather than a particular technical approach or algorithm.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that we don’t really agree on what counts as a model of the world. At a very broad level, any system that learns useful regularities from data has some model of the world. A language model knows a lot about how things relate to each other. Does that make it a world model? If we use that definition, the term becomes so broad that it’s not very useful.

But then you can make the definition much narrower. Maybe a world model needs to predict how an environment will change, including what happens when you take an action. Now we’re talking about something you can use for planning. Even there, what should it predict? Every pixel in the next frame, or just the information that matters for a decision? Those are very different requirements.

And we don’t have a single, clear test. A system might generate a very convincing video but still get a basic physical interaction wrong. So looking realistic and understanding how the world works aren’t necessarily the same thing.

For me, the useful starting point is: what do you want this model to let you do? Predict, interact, plan? Once you specify that, you can have a much more concrete conversation about what it needs to learn and how to measure it.

r001.rationale: The response says definitions vary with what a model should predict or enable, but it does not explain that “world model” names a goal rather than a particular technical approach or algorithm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that “world” is such a broad word, and “model” is also a very broad word. Different people use the same term to describe different capabilities. Are we talking about predicting the next video frame? Understanding how physical objects interact? Or learning an environment well enough that an agent can plan and act in it? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

For me, a useful way to approach it is to ask what the model lets you do. If it can generate a plausible future, does that mean it understands how the world works? What happens if you take a different action? Can it predict the consequences, including situations it hasn’t seen before? That’s a much stronger requirement than producing something that looks realistic.

So I think the term is hard to define because we haven’t agreed on the capability we want to capture. I’d rather make the question concrete: what does the model represent, what can it predict, and how can we test whether those predictions are useful for acting in the world?

r001.rationale: The response says “world” and “model” are broad and that people mean different capabilities, but it does not explain that world models name a goal rather than a specific technical approach or algorithm.
